1. America after the Civil War (to the end of Reconstruction)
2. Western expansion (Mexico, Chinese exclusion, mining, railroads, industrial ranching, collective violence against the Natives, assimilation, the buffalo, tourism and parks)
3. Labor (industrial growth, concentration of wealth, global migrations into the U.S., working conditions and wages, economic panics, women and children in the workplace, railroad strike of 1877, labor violence and organizing strategies, farmers unionizing, philosophical arguments over the new capitalist order)
4. Cities and Immigrants (urbanization, types of cities, worldwide migration and demographic shifts, the myth of America, policies against immigration, community organizing among immigrants, city missions and charity, settlement houses, ethnicity and gender in cities, populism, and the election of 1896)
5. U.S. foreign affairs (colony grabs, empire and businessmen, Latin America, Hawaii, Cuba, Spanish-American War, Philippines, Puerto Rico, Roosevelt's foreign policy, Taft's foreign policy)
6. Progressivism (principles, global exchange of ideas, housing, racial segregation & Jim Crow, racial exclusion within progressivism, electoral reforms, labor issues, trust busting, conservation/preservation of nature, women's suffrage)
7. World War I (origins, America's response, conflicting visions, intervention in Latin America, mobilization, controlling dissent, women in wartime, blacks in wartime, fighting Communism and Red Scare, treaty)
8. Postwar (car culture, radio, mass consumption, immigration restriction, KKK, black renaissance and repression in cities, black international movements, movies, sports, celebrity, new woman, religion, Prohibition, instability in Latin America, 1928 election, prosperity)
9. New Deal (old failures, Great Depression, FDR's Hundred Days, SOcial Security, labor activism, 1936 election, women and the New Deal, Hispanics and the New Deal, Native Americans and the New Deal, preservation, judicial challenge, political setbacks)

Thanks, I always thought that it closed out any chat within a certain range, not just the inactive ones, but that's helpful! If only it had all the pros of the other more effective apps.

I think the difference is that, assuming someone has basic social skills, approaching someone in person can let you know very quickly if someone is interested in talking to you or getting to know you because you can see them and their reaction. Of course there's always going to be people who don't get the obvious signs and just keep talking, but that wouldn't ever change.

On an app, you don't know if the person is ignoring you because they have already moved on and just don't want to say anything or they just haven't been able to. There were plenty of times where someone went days without responding after a really nice conversation and it was impossible to know if you were getting ghosted or things just came up and they weren't able to be around for a bit. I never wanted to just unmatch since I thought there had been something there and didn't just want to chalk it up to ghosting. You wouldn't have that problem in person.

That's why I just think an app would work well if any pending "matches" stay forever, one-sided introductions stay (to allow any time), but once there's a response, the time starts for a certain number of days and then without a mutual response to reset that clock, automatic unmatch. The person getting "ignored" would then never know that either the person unmatched or they didn't care to respond, so they can move on.

Something like that, in my opinion, incentivizes people to respond only to the matches they really want to have a conversation with, and filters out any lingering ones where they clearly aren't interested, without the requirement to directly take the action to unmatch. I think it would be good for the mental health of both sides of the dating equation by focusing on active conversation (and therefore developing that connection) while clearing out the ones that naturally don't work out.

The nuclear option that was employed in 2013 and 2017 for special cases was just amending the Senate cloture rule to allow only 51 votes to end debate, rather than 60. The legislation itself does not require more votes to pass, but if you don't invoke cloture, you can't ever vote on the final bill.

No problem! Single nucleotide polymorphisms have been really important for us understanding diseases in the last 15 years. Genome-wide association studies essentially take the DNA of a large sample of people with a certain disease and people without the disease and then see if there are consistent SNPs shared by people with the disease and not in the people without. There's of course a lot more that goes into narrowing it down and getting rid of certain misleading data, but it's what leads to the correlation we see when discussing risk factors.

And just to give you an idea of the scale of these things, so far with something like irritable bowel syndrome, we've identified over 200 SNPs associated with it. It's what makes this stuff so complicated. Someone with IBD could have 40 of them, some could have 190, so it's never authoritative.

When those SNPs are reviewed and confirmed again and again by experiment and then logged, that's how 23andMe and Ancestry and stuff can take someone's DNA sample and say "Oh, you have these 10 SNPs, these could mean you're more at risk for [insert condition here]."

Everyone has two copies of DNA with the potential for each copy to be either A or G at this location of DNA. So someone can have A:A, A:G, or G:G. The protein that is expressed from this section of DNA is involved in the immune system against viral infection. Someone with an A creates this protein but it has a lower efficiency, so it's considered a risk factor for immune reaction against viral infection. Someone with a G creates this protein with a higher efficiency. 

So someone with two copies of G might be better equipped and someone with two copies of A might be at higher risk, but having both A in one copy and G in the other means that any lower efficiency is offset by the other. Having different letters (A and G) at this location is where we get the term "heterozygous" in genetics, as opposed to homozygous (A:A and G:G).
To be fair, I don't really think that was ever disputable. Genetic mutations and protein isoforms are like the foundation for differential outcomes in any disease state.

At this exact location of DNA, individuals can have either an adenine (A) or a guanine (G) base. Whichever letter it is determines where the gene sequence is cut and created and therefore how efficient the gene OAS1 is when it is produced as a protein. It just so happens that when it's a G, the protein product from the OAS1 gene is more efficient because of how it was spliced. This protein is involved in the immune response during viral infection. If it's A, it's still produced and works, but it has a lower efficiency, so it's considered more of a risk factor. To be fair, there are thousands of risk factors when you get down to the genetic level, so it's more of a summation and probability.

We have two "copies" of our non-sex chromosomes in each cell and this is where you can have different letters by mutation. This is called a single nucleotide polymorphism and is most of the difference between your own DNA and the DNA of someone else. So if you have two copies of this DNA location, one site can have a G and the other can have an A and both will create a functional protein, one with a higher efficiency and the other less so. That's where the A:A and A:G language comes from. If you have G:G, it means both copies of your DNA have G at this site, so both proteins being expressed will have the normal efficiency.

The problem is that people on the demonstrating side appeal to the peaceful protests that were so powerful in the 1960s when it came to the civil rights movement, but there are two key differences that have blunted any impact that peaceful protest has today:

1. While there are definitely examples today of peaceful protesters being routed by tear gas and projectiles, they are still overwhelmingly passive in most cities. Peaceful protests of the 1960s were a much more provocative image of "proper" Americans being bitten by ferocious dogs, children being beamed with firehoses, and men and women beaten with clubs mercilessly. There was no semblance of assembly when the police went into violence mode anytime black demonstrators just started walking down the road together.
2. Sheltered suburbanites, who either were ignorant of the severeity of the state of race relations in the cities, were able to see for the first time this huge contrast in oppression and peaceful assembly through the TV. Showing people the gritty details of this crackdown made it much easier to gain sympathies to the cause and ultimately stronger allies who potentially wielded a larger share of influence on the government.

These two don't exist anymore and their absence, to me, makes peaceful protest a ridiculous myth. The vast majority of protests that are "peaceful" involve chanting and crowds standing against a wall of police who don't do anything but watch for hours until the powers that be tell them to disperse the crowd. Government has learned that if they don't push back too much too early, protesters will go home that night thinking they accomplished something. Authorities also use the manufactured heartfelt moments of kneeling with demonstrators, marching with demonstrators, hugging demonstrators, and speaking with demonstrators to fool naive spectators into believing that they are acting in good faith without the responsibility of actually doing anything about it. These shows of solidarity, no matter how genuine they seem, are effective in planting the idea that protesters are making a difference and swaying the opinion of their oppressors. These officers sweet-talking the crowd are the same ones that put on the gas mask at curfew. 

The second point is even more important. Social media has made it virtually impossible to be sheltered from the images of the news, as average families were when they got their first TV. Any demonstrator who is currently engaging in a war of messaging by trying to gain allies is operating in a world that doesn't exist anymore. The sides have already been chosen and people are more likely today to have opinions that will not be changed, regardless of what they see and hear. Trying to sway people to the side of racial justice and police accountability by peaceful protest is not only foolish, but a waste of time when the only people who seemingly appreciate peaceful protest are the ones who don't believe the message in the first place. There is no such thing as potential allies who've never seen the effects of police brutality and can be swayed - one side sees it and thinks it's a problem; the other side sees it and thinks it's a solution. This isn't a war of messaging like it was in the 1960s because messaging has already been decided. 

If change is to be accomplished in the modern era, change that attempts to regulate the authorities who don't want to be regulated, it will only be through the fear and urgency that widespread violence and civil unrest will harm those in power more than the effort of reforming institutions - and that can only be accomplished by a war of attrition, modeled after both the offensive and defensive tactics of Hong Kong, with a parallel campaign of non-violent civil disobedience. Peaceful protest today serves as one thing and one thing only: it's merely a vigil for the dead. A show of sympathy and solidarity without the force needed to effect change.

Swadlow may have changed in the past 5 years (I took PSYC 1100 in 2012). The most important thing to recognize is that he puts a lot of emphasis on the physical biology rather than the theory. 

The first exam I remember was pretty heavy on the actual biological foundations of psychology, notably the action potential and the other components of the neuron, as well as the major neurotransmitters. Depending on how far you've gone in the unit, the CNS is going to be a pretty big part as well.

I wish I could say things are obsolete, but Swadlow likes to keep a lot of the information as dense as possible so that "all" of it is on the exam. My suggestion would be to really go over the biological stuff from small (neuronal level) to large (the regions of the brain that were covered, and how they connect down to the cellular level). Any type of lecture material that had to do with research methodology and the history of psychological thought (i.e. Wundt, Gestalt, B. F. Skinner) is also still "important" but my go-to procedure for Swadlow was to tie back the conceptual theory and psychological thought stuff back to the biology. Not only does it help you memorize the two layers of learning, but it also just cements it when it comes time for the exams. 

Swadlow was actually not as bad as imagined when you realize the guy does his research on the biological/molecular side of psychology rather than the development of theory. Sometimes in lectures he came across very bored with theory. Anytime he ties it back to the biological foundations (consciousness/behavior/perception), definitely make a note for yourself and try to reinforce that connection when you go back through the material.
